unit.title: Check/identify/isolate/rectify malfunctioning electrical machinery appliances and fixtures

summary: This unit teaches you to lead the checking, diagnosis, isolation and repair of faulty appliances, motors, fans, heaters, air-conditioners and light fittings. You will learn to prepare from the maker's data, take faulty equipment out of service safely, test motors, capacitors and heating elements with the supply off, work out what the readings should be, rectify the fault like for like, test and return the equipment, and advise the customer on repair or replacement.

blocks.p: Households, hotels, farms and workshops in Jamaica depend on equipment that runs for years in heat, damp and salt air and on a supply that is not always steady. When it fails, the customer wants it working quickly, but a hasty repair can leave a motor overheating, a heater leaking current to earth or a machine live. This unit is for Level 3 trainees who take charge of the repair: they find out what happened, make the equipment safe, test it with the supply off, decide what is wrong, repair it properly, and explain the result to the customer in plain words. Plug-in appliances and fixed equipment are both covered.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Prepare for the job
Ask what the equipment did, find its model, age and history, and get the maker's service data before you go.
Make faulty equipment safe
Unplug or isolate it, lock off, prove dead at the equipment, tag it 'Do not use' and allow for heat, movement and stored charge.
Inspect first
Look for burnt parts, loose wires, water, corrosion and insects before any test.
Test the supply-off
Use continuity, resistance, insulation resistance, capacitance and earth tests, and compare each with the expected value.
Diagnose motors
Read winding resistances, find open, shorted and earthed windings, bad capacitors, stuck centrifugal switches, worn bearings and overheating.
Diagnose appliances and fixtures
Find the cause in heaters, cookers, fridges, washing machines, pumps, fans, air-conditioners, LED and fluorescent fittings and outdoor lights.
Rectify like for like
Replace the faulty part with one of the same rating, remake joints properly, and never bypass a protective device.
Test and return to service
Dead tests, then the authorised person's function test, measuring the running current against the nameplate.
Advise on repair or replace
Give the customer the costs and the risks, in J$ with GCT at the current rate, and leave the choice to them.
Lead, record and report
Run a repair bench, check trainees, keep job cards and give a clear report.

blocks.note: Much equipment in Jamaica is made for the US market (115 V or 230 V, 60 Hz) but runs on **110/220 V, 50 Hz**. Check the nameplate for voltage and frequency. A motor made for 60 Hz may run hot and slow on 50 Hz; a heater made for 115 V will work, with slightly less power. Never fit a 110 V item to 220 V.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: At the Centre, trainees test equipment **dead**. Only the instructor (the authorised person) energises it, on a protected bench supply, and measures running current. This kit explains the live readings, because you must understand them, but you do not take them until you are authorised.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Preparing for the job and making the equipment safe

ul: **Ask what happened.** What did it do, when did it start, was it working just before a storm, a power cut or cleaning, did it trip the breaker, make a noise or smell, spark?

**Find the equipment's details**: make, model, age, and any past repairs. Get the **maker's service data**: winding resistances, capacitor values, test points, parts lists. Textbook figures and what a plumber or a neighbour remembers are not a substitute.

**Bring the right tools**: a two-pole tester and proving unit, a multimeter with a capacitance range, a low-resistance ohmmeter, an insulation resistance tester, a capacitor discharge tool, insulated hand tools, spare common parts and tags.
**Plan around the customer**: a hotel, a clinic or a restaurant needs to know how long the equipment will be out, and may need a temporary arrangement.

flow: Switch off at the equipment's own switch, if it is safe to reach
Unplug it, or isolate at the isolator or breaker and lock off
Fix a tag: 'Do not use', with the date and your name
Prove dead at the equipment's terminals, with the tester checked before and after
Allow for heat, moving parts and stored charge

head: Situation
What to do straight away
rows: A plug-in appliance sparks, smokes or smells hot
Unplug it (if you can do so safely), tag it 'Do not use', take it out of service. Do not keep using it 'until the job is finished'.
A fixed machine is smoking or sparking at night

By phone, tell the owner not to touch it, to switch it off at the breaker if that is safe, to keep people away and not to switch it on again; call 110 if there is fire. On arrival, isolate, lock, tag and prove dead before anything else.
Several appliances fail together after a storm

Suspect the supply: a surge, a high voltage from a lost neutral or a fault at the service. Check the voltage at the outlet (authorised person), the neutral at the meter and main board, before blaming the appliances. Report supply faults to JPS.
Equipment that has been flooded
Do not switch on. Dry out by an approved method, test insulation resistance, and replace anything that cannot be restored.

ul: **Capacitors** in motors, fans, air-conditioners, fridges and electronic equipment hold a charge. Measure the voltage across them and discharge them with a resistor tool before you touch the terminals; never short a capacitor with a screwdriver.
**Heat**: elements, water heaters, motors and lamps stay hot. Allow time to cool.
**Movement**: a motor or fan that was running keeps turning for a while, and a fan can be turned by the wind. Wait until everything stops.
**Pressure and refrigerant**: only a certified refrigeration technician opens a refrigerant circuit.
**Weight and height**: fans, fittings and air-conditioners are heavy and often high; use safe access.

blocks.note: Never test a motor-driven machine that has been running a minute ago without allowing for hot surfaces and parts that are still turning.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Inspecting, testing and the expected readings

blocks.p: Many faults are found by eye before any instrument is used: burnt or discoloured wires and terminals, melted plastic, cracked casings, loose or broken wires, water marks and rust, insect nests, damaged cords and plugs, a bulging capacitor, an oil stain. Look, smell and feel (when dead and cool). A visible cause tells you where to test, and the tests can be skipped only if the cause is certain.

head: Test
Instrument
What it shows
rows: Continuity / resistance
Ohmmeter or multimeter, leads nulled
Whether a winding, element, switch, fuse or wire is whole, open or shorted
Insulation resistance (IR)
Insulation tester at 500 V DC (lower for electronic parts; follow the maker)
Leakage from conductors to earth or to the body
Capacitance
Multimeter with a capacitance range, or a capacitance meter, after discharging
Whether a capacitor still has its marked value
Earth continuity
Low-resistance ohmmeter
Whether a Class I body is properly earthed
Polarity
Ohmmeter or tester
Switches and fuses are in the line
Running current (authorised person)
Clamp meter on one conductor
How hard the motor or heater is working, compared with the nameplate
Thermal imaging (authorised person)
Thermal camera
Hot joints and overloaded parts without touching them

head: To find
Formula
Example
rows: Element resistance
R = V² ÷ P
Element power
P = V² ÷ R
A 110 V element reading 12.1 Ω: 110 × 110 ÷ 12.1 = 1,000 W
Current
I = P ÷ V
A 2,500 W heater on 220 V: 11.4 A
Percentage over the nameplate
(measured − rated) ÷ rated × 100
Rated 8 A, measured 10 A: 2 ÷ 8 × 100 = 25% over
Capacitor tolerance limits
Marked value ± the percentage
Single-phase compressor windings
S–R = C–R + C–S
C–R 2.5 Ω and C–S 4 Ω: S–R should be 6.5 Ω

blocks.note: A cold filament lamp reads far less than its working resistance, but a nickel-chrome heater element reads close to its working value. A heating element's cold reading is therefore a good test.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Reading
Meaning
rows: OL or infinity across a winding, element or fuse
Open circuit: broken wire, burnt element, blown fuse
Much lower than the expected value
Shorted turns or a short across the part
Higher than expected, or unsteady
A poor joint, corrosion or a damaged strand
Low IR to the body or sheath (well under 1 MΩ)
Leakage: damp, damaged insulation, a broken-down element sheath; it trips GFCIs and RCDs
Good winding resistance but low IR
Insulation fault to earth, not a broken winding

head: Type
How it starts and runs
Used on
rows: Capacitor-start
A start winding with a **start capacitor** gives the starting torque; a **centrifugal switch** opens at about 75–80% of full speed and takes the start winding out
Pumps, compressors, bench machines
Capacitor-start, capacitor-run
As above, with a run capacitor left in circuit after starting
Larger pumps and compressors
Permanent split capacitor (PSC)
A run capacitor stays in series with the auxiliary winding all the time; no switch
Ceiling and extractor fans, small pumps, air-conditioner fans
Shaded-pole
A copper ring on each pole gives a weak starting torque
Small fans, extractors
Universal (brushes)
Brushes and a commutator; runs on AC or DC
Drills, grinders, blenders

blocks.p: The motor has a **run (main) winding** that is in circuit all the time it runs, and a **start (auxiliary) winding**. On a hermetic compressor the terminals are marked **C** (common), **R** (run) and **S** (start). Resistances add: the S–R reading equals the C–R reading plus the C–S reading. The start winding usually has the higher resistance.

head: Symptom
Likely causes
Tests
rows: Hums, does not start
Start capacitor open or weak; centrifugal switch stuck open; start winding open; seized bearing or load
Capacitor measurement; switch contacts; winding resistances; turn the shaft by hand
Starts, then runs hot and the overload trips
Centrifugal switch stuck **closed**, so the start winding stays in and burns; overloaded machine; shorted turns; low voltage
Switch contacts at rest and operated by hand; windings; running current (authorised person)
Runs slowly or weakly (fans)
Weak run capacitor; worn bearings; shorted turns
Capacitance against the marked value; shaft by hand; winding resistances
Stops after a few minutes and restarts by itself when cool
The built-in **thermal protector** is opening because the motor is overheating
Find the cause: load, ventilation, voltage, bearings, windings; do not bypass the protector
Rumbling or grinding, worse over weeks
Worn bearings
Shaft feels rough or loose when turned by hand
Trips the GFCI
Winding insulation to frame is low: damp, damage, flooding
IR winding to frame
Smells burnt, sparks (brush motors)
Worn brushes, damaged commutator
Brush length, commutator surface

ol: Isolate, prove dead and **discharge** the capacitor through a resistor tool; check with a meter that the voltage is gone.
Disconnect it from the circuit before measuring.
Measure with a capacitance meter. Compare with the marked value and its tolerance: run capacitors are often ± 5% or ± 10%.
Replace if it is outside the tolerance, bulging, leaking or showing signs of heat.

The replacement must have the **same µF** and at least the same **voltage rating**, and be of the same kind (run or start). A different value changes the motor's current and torque; a higher value does not make it 'run faster'.

blocks.p: A **dual run capacitor** has three terminals: **C** (common), **FAN** and **HERM**. HERM goes to the compressor (hermetic motor) and FAN to the outdoor fan motor; each section has its own µF value.

ul: The three windings should have **nearly equal** resistance. Two normal readings and one much lower (for example 3.2, 3.2 and 2.1 Ω) show **shorted turns** in the low winding. One open (OL) winding shows a broken winding or a loose link.
A winding with shorted turns draws extra current, makes the motor unbalanced and overheats it, and the overload trips. **Do not set the overload higher.** The motor is rewound or replaced.
Good winding readings with low IR mean the insulation to frame has failed.
A wrong rotation after repair is cured by swapping any two lines, with the motor isolated.
A motor that was flooded or left damp gives a low IR. Dry it by an approved method (an oven or gentle heating as the maker allows, not running it), then retest. Never run a damp motor to dry it out.

blocks.note: When a motor runs hotter than normal, compare its running current (measured by the authorised person) with the nameplate. Do not fit a larger overload to stop it tripping: the motor will burn out instead.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Heaters, cookers, refrigerators, pumps and washing machines

head: Symptom
Likely causes
Tests (supply off)
rows: No heat
Open element; open thermostat; tripped high-limit cut-out; loose or burnt connection
Element end to end against R = V² ÷ P; thermostat and cut-out continuity; terminals
Trips the GFCI when heating
Element sheath has broken down: leakage to earth
IR from the element terminals to the sheath or tank earth
High-limit cut-out has tripped
Stuck thermostat, scaling, dry-firing or poor water flow
**Find why it tripped before resetting it.** Test the thermostat; check the water circuit.
One hob ring stays at full heat
The ring's **energy regulator** (simmerstat) has stuck closed
Regulator contacts operated by hand
One element on a stove is dead
Open element or its connection
Element resistance; terminal block for burning
Water heater makes a rumbling sound
Scale on the element
Inspect when drained

ul: A water heater tank must be **full of water** before it is switched on: a dry element burns out in seconds. The plumber drains and refills it when an element is changed.
A replacement element has the same **voltage and wattage**, and a new gasket.
A cooker has high currents: tighten terminals to torque, and replace any burnt terminal block and the damaged conductor ends.
A compressor that clicks, tries to start and stops every few minutes points to the **start relay** or the **overload protector** (and sometimes the run capacitor).
A compressor that does not start and hums may have an open start circuit or a seized compressor.
Check the thermostat, the defrost heater and timer, and the door switch, which can leave a light or fan running.
A leak or a seized compressor is refrigeration work: the electrician hands over to a certified technician.

A pump that **switches on and off every few seconds** with one tap open usually has lost the air charge in its **pressure tank**, so the pressure switch cycles. It is a plumbing fault, not an electrical one.
A pump that hums and does not turn: capacitor, seized impeller or a blocked pump.
A pump that trips the GFCI: motor insulation, damp terminal box, damaged cable.
A machine that will not start a cycle and whose door-lock light never comes on usually has a faulty **door lock (interlock)**. The interlock is a safety device: it is replaced, never bridged.
No water: inlet valve or its solenoid. No drain: drain pump. Noisy drum: bearings.

blocks.h: Class I and Class II appliances

blocks.p: A metal-cased **Class I** appliance needs a good earth: test **earth continuity** from the plug's earth pin to the case. A **Class II** appliance carries the double-square symbol, is double insulated and has no earth, so no earth test is made. Both get an insulation resistance test.

ol: Ask what happened. Check that the thermostat is calling for cooling and the remote has batteries.
Isolate the outdoor unit at its isolator and breaker, lock off, tag and prove dead at its terminals.
Inspect for burnt wires, insect nests in the contactor, corrosion (common in salt air), and water in the electrical box.
Discharge and measure the **run capacitor**. On a dual capacitor, HERM serves the compressor and FAN the fan.
Check the contactor: coil resistance, and contacts that are burnt or stuck.
Measure the compressor windings (C–R, C–S, S–R) and IR to earth; check the fan motor.
Replace faulty electrical parts like for like.

head: Symptom
Likely electrical causes
rows: Indoor fan runs, outdoor unit does not start
Outdoor contactor or its coil; run capacitor; fan or compressor winding; a tripped overload; wiring from the indoor unit
Outdoor fan runs, compressor does not
HERM section of the capacitor; compressor start components; compressor windings
Trips the breaker as the compressor starts
Shorted or earthed compressor winding; wrong breaker size; weak capacitor
Does not cool, everything runs
Usually refrigerant, dirty coils or filters: not the electrician's work

blocks.note: The electrician must not open the refrigerant circuit. A compressor that is seized, an oil stain at a pipe joint or any refrigerant leak is handed to a certified refrigeration technician. Compressors and inverter boards can also hold a charge: wait the time on the label and measure before you touch them.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: A ceiling fan that runs **slowly on every speed**, with smooth bearings, usually has a weak **fan capacitor**: measure it and replace it with the same µF and voltage.
Wobble and noise are balance, blade or mounting problems; check the mounting is secure before testing electrically.
A fan that works on some speeds only: the regulator or the speed winding taps.

head: Fitting
Fault
Likely cause
Fix
rows: LED panel or tube
Flickers, then goes out after minutes; LED board is undamaged
The **LED driver** (heat in a ceiling void is a common cause)
Replace with a driver matching the LED board's current and voltage
Switch-start fluorescent
Ends glow but never lights fully
The starter; sometimes the tube or ballast
Replace the starter, then the tube; consider converting to LED
Fluorescent with an electronic ballast
Does not light, or flickers at the ends
Tube at end of life; ballast
Replace the tube, then the ballast
Outdoor security light, corroded green lamp holder
Keeps failing
Salt and damp; wrong IP rating
Replace with a fitting rated for coastal outdoor use, with sealed cable entries
Dusk-to-dawn light
Stays on all day
The **photocell** (light sensor) has failed or is covered or wrongly aimed
Check the photocell first
Any fitting
Stays off with a good lamp
Open line, switch, holder or driver
Dead continuity tests

blocks.p: **IP ratings** (ingress protection): the first digit is protection from solids and the second from water. IP65 is dust-tight and protected against water jets; for a seaside villa choose a rating suited to the place and a corrosion-resistant body. Old fluorescent tubes contain mercury: keep them whole and take them to an approved recycler.

sections.title: Rectifying the fault, testing and returning to service

head: Rule
Why
rows: Replace like for like: same voltage, rating, type and size
A part that fits is not necessarily the right part. A thermal protector, fuse or overload relay protects the equipment; a wrong one removes that protection.
Never bridge or bypass a protector, interlock or cut-out
The protection is the last line of defence.
Find the cause before resetting or replacing
A reset hides a stuck thermostat; a new fuse hides a short.
Remake joints on clean, bright copper with proper terminals, tightened to torque
Heated, loose joints are common faults.
Keep the faulty parts and show them to the customer
It shows what failed and why they are being charged.
Do not 'fix' with tape, paint or spray
They do not restore a joint or insulation.

flow: Visual check: parts fitted like for like, terminals tight, covers and guards on, no tools left inside
Dead tests: earth continuity (Class I), insulation resistance, polarity
Tools out; locks removed by their owners
Authorised person restores the supply, everyone clear
Function test: starts, runs the right way, no unusual noise or vibration, controls and stops work
Running current compared with the nameplate; GFCI tested

blocks.p: A running current more than the nameplate figure (for example 10 A against 8 A, which is 25% over) shows the machine is overloaded or faulty and must be investigated. A wrong direction of rotation is corrected with the supply isolated.

ul: Find the exact fault first, with the equipment isolated. If it is the compressor or a refrigerant leak, a certified refrigeration technician gives that quote.
Compare the **full cost of the repair** (parts, labour and GCT at the current rate) with the cost of a **new item delivered**.
A common guide is that if the repair costs more than about half of a new item's price, replacing is often better value, especially for old equipment.
Also consider: the age and remaining life of the equipment, its energy use against a new efficient model, the cost of losing stock or service if it fails again, and the warranty on a new one.
Give the owner the figures in writing, in J$, explain them in plain words, and **let them decide**.

blocks.note: Explain a fault to a customer who is not technical in plain words: what failed, why it failed, and the choices. Do not blame the customer, and do not use technical terms to impress.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Running a repair bench, records and handover

ul: **Book in** each item with a job card: customer, item, fault reported, a number; tag it so it cannot be used by mistake. Store waiting items in a marked area.
**Order the jobs** by urgency and safety, agreed with customers, not by what is easiest or which customer phones most often. Match each job to the trainee's skill, with the maker's data.

**Control the test supply.** Only the authorised person or the instructor switches on the bench supply; every item is unplugged or isolated before it is opened; capacitors are discharged and hot parts cooled.
**Check** each repair before the item is reassembled, watch the dead tests, and run the function test yourself.
**Record** the parts used and the time for billing; give finished items a pass label and a short report; label items that cannot be repaired and tell the customer.

head: Entry
Example of a useful one
rows: Fault found
Fan capacitor 2.5 µF measured 1.4 µF; fan ran slowly on all speeds
Repair
Capacitor replaced with 2.5 µF, 450 V; terminals tightened
Tests
IR 150 MΩ; earth continuity 0.2 Ω; fan tested at all speeds by the instructor, running current 0.35 A
Advice
Fan bearings are dry and noisy; oil at the next service

blocks.p: 'Fan fixed and working again' tells the next person nothing. Give the customer a job report with the fault, the repair, the tests and the advice. Show them the old parts. Do not leave the old parts inside the machine or the test instruments behind.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can prepare for a repair by asking what happened and getting the maker's service data.
I can take faulty equipment out of service safely, tag it and prove dead, and allow for capacitors, heat and movement.
I can say what to do by phone and on arrival when a machine is sparking or smoking.
I can suspect a supply fault when several appliances fail together after a storm.
I can inspect before testing, and choose the right test for each fault.
I can work out element resistance and power, and the percentage of a measured current over the nameplate.
I can discharge, measure and replace a capacitor, and read the C, FAN and HERM terminals.
I can read single-phase compressor winding resistances and check S–R = C–R + C–S.
I can diagnose a capacitor-start motor that hums, or starts and overheats, and a motor with a thermal protector.
I can recognise shorted turns from three-phase winding readings, and say why the overload is not raised.
I can find the cause of a heater tripping a GFCI, a tripped high-limit cut-out and a ring stuck at full heat.
I can check the electrical side of an air-conditioner, and say where my work ends.
I can diagnose LED, fluorescent and outdoor light faults and recommend the fix.
I can rectify like for like, never bypass protection, and test before and after switch-on.
I can advise on repair or replace, run a repair bench and write a useful job card.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: R = V² ÷ P
Element resistance from its rating
S–R = C–R + C–S
Windings of a single-phase compressor
About 75–80% of speed
Where a centrifugal switch normally opens
About half the price of a new item
A common guide for repair against replace
500 V DC, at least 1 MΩ
A usual IR test voltage and minimum; follow the maker for electronic parts

terms: Capacitor-start motor
A single-phase motor that uses a start capacitor and a centrifugal switch to start.
Centrifugal switch
A switch inside a motor that opens at about 75–80% of speed and takes the start winding out of circuit.
Dual run capacitor
A capacitor with C, FAN and HERM terminals, serving a compressor and a fan.
Energy regulator
A control on a hob ring that switches it on and off to set its heat.
HERM
The capacitor terminal that goes to the hermetic compressor.
High-limit cut-out
A safety device that cuts off a water heater if it gets far too hot and must be reset by hand.
IP rating
A code for how well a fitting resists dust and water.
LED driver
The electronic unit that changes mains power to the low-voltage DC for the LEDs.
Like for like
A replacement with the same voltage, rating, type and size.
Photocell
A light sensor that switches an outdoor light on at dusk and off at dawn.
Run winding
The winding of a single-phase motor that stays in circuit all the time it runs.
Shorted turns
Winding turns that touch each other, lowering the winding's resistance and overheating it.
Thermal protector
A built-in device that opens the supply to a motor when it overheats.
Thermal imaging camera
An instrument that shows heat as a picture, so hot joints can be found without touching.

c1.title: A water heater and a kettle in a Treasure Beach guest house
c1.text: A guest house at Treasure Beach, St Elizabeth, has a 220 V, 2,500 W storage water heater on a two-pole breaker. Guests report no hot water, and the owner, Miss Marcia Walters, says the breaker has not tripped. A GFCI protects the circuit. Trainee leader Dennis isolates the heater, locks off, tags it and proves dead at the heater's terminals. He disconnects the element and finds that its resistance, measured end to end, is OL. In the kitchen, a 110 V kettle with a 1,000 W element will not heat at all.

c2.title: A pool pump motor in Montego Bay
c2.text: A hotel pool in Montego Bay has a single-phase 220 V capacitor-start pump motor that hums and does not start. It is isolated and proved dead. Maintenance trainee Rushane discharges the start capacitor and measures it: the label reads 88–108 µF, 250 V, and the meter reads 12 µF. The centrifugal switch contacts read about 0.5 Ω at rest. The shaft turns freely by hand. The windings read: C to R 2.4 Ω, C to S 3.6 Ω, S to R 6.0 Ω.

c3.title: A split air-conditioner in a Savanna-la-Mar office
c3.text: A small office in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, reports that its split air-conditioner blows warm air. The indoor fan runs, but the outdoor unit is silent. The unit is 90 metres from the sea. Trainee leader Joel isolates and proves the outdoor unit dead, and finds white powder on the contactor's contacts and an ants' nest inside the box. The dual run capacitor is marked 45 + 5 µF, 370 V, with terminals C, HERM and FAN; HERM measures 45 µF and FAN measures 5 µF.

c4.title: Mixed repairs at a Mandeville workshop
c4.text: At a repair workshop in Mandeville, Manchester, trainee leader Tiana has four jobs: a three-phase 400 V extractor motor whose overload trips after a few minutes, with winding readings of 6.1 Ω, 6.0 Ω and 3.4 Ω; a washing machine that will not begin its cycle although water is in the drum and the door-lock light never comes on; an LED light panel that has started to flicker and then switches off; and a freezer whose compressor clicks and cuts out every few minutes. A customer has asked Tiana to simply 'put in a bigger overload' on the extractor.

c5.title: A freezer for a Mandeville restaurant
c5.text: A small restaurant in Mandeville asks you whether to repair or replace its 10-year-old chest freezer. Its compressor has burnt out and a certified refrigeration technician quotes J$ 34,000 plus GCT for a replacement compressor, gas and labour. A new, similar freezer costs J$ 62,000 plus GCT delivered. The freezer holds about J$ 80,000 of stock.

questions.q: What does the OL reading from the element tell Dennis?
o: The element is open circuit: its heating wire is broken
The element is healthy but its insulation to earth has failed
The element is shorted, so the breaker would have tripped
The meter is on the wrong range and must be changed
questions.why: OL means no path through the element, so the wire is broken and no current can flow: there is no heat, and nothing for the breaker or GFCI to trip on. A shorted element would read far below the expected value, and an insulation failure would show on an IR test, not on end-to-end resistance.

questions.q: Disconnected and cold, a healthy 220 V, 2,500 W water-heater element should read about what?
o: About 88 Ω
About 19 Ω
About 11 Ω
About 0.1 Ω
questions.why: R = V² ÷ P = 220 × 220 ÷ 2,500 = 48,400 ÷ 2,500 = 19.4 Ω. 11 would be the current in amps (2,500 ÷ 220 = 11.4), not a resistance.

questions.q: What must be done before the supply is restored after the new element is fitted?
o: Test the element's glow, by switching it on dry for a few seconds
Have the plumber refill the tank, so the element is under water
Fit a larger breaker, since a new element draws more
Reset the high-limit cut-out a second time, to be sure
questions.why: An element switched on without water burns out in seconds. The plumber drains the tank for the change and refills it, and the tank stays full before any power is restored. A new element of the same rating draws the same current, so the breaker stays as it was.

questions.q: What reading is expected for the kettle's element, and what does the kettle's failure to heat suggest?
o: About 12 Ω; an OL reading means the element or a series part is open
About 120 Ω; an OL reading means the kettle has been left unplugged
About 1.2 Ω; an OL reading means that the element has shorted
About 12 Ω; an OL reading means that the cord is far too thin
questions.why: R = 110 × 110 ÷ 1,000 = 12.1 Ω. An OL reading means the element, or a series part such as a thermal fuse or thermostat, is open. Test each part separately; a short would read far below 12 Ω.

questions.q: What does the 12 µF reading tell Rushane about the start capacitor?
o: It is within tolerance, because the capacitor still has some charge
It is far below its 88 µF minimum, so it must be replaced
It is normal, because capacitors lose value when the motor runs
It shows the centrifugal switch has stuck closed
questions.why: A start capacitor must measure between the two marked values, 88–108 µF. 12 µF is a fraction of that, so the motor cannot develop starting torque and just hums. The new capacitor has the same µF range and at least the same voltage.

questions.q: Rushane tests the motor's three terminals and records C–R 2.4 Ω, C–S 3.6 Ω and S–R 6.0 Ω. How should he read this?
o: Healthy windings, because 2.4 + 3.6 = 6.0
A shorted start winding, because C to S is the higher reading
An open run winding, because C to S and C to R are not equal
A run winding with shorted turns, because S to R is so high
questions.why: For a single-phase compressor or motor, S–R should equal C–R plus C–S. Here 2.4 + 3.6 = 6.0, so the windings are whole and in step. The start winding normally reads higher than the run winding, so 3.6 Ω against 2.4 Ω is expected.

questions.q: Rushane has only a 50 µF, 250 V capacitor in the van and suggests fitting it 'so the motor starts harder'. What is the right decision?
o: Fit it, since a larger capacitor gives more starting torque safely
Fit it, and add a second 50 µF capacitor in series with it
Get one with a value in the marked 88–108 µF range
Fit it, and turn the overload relay down to protect the motor
questions.why: The capacitor value is chosen to give the right phase shift and starting torque for that motor. Too small a value cannot start the pump; too large a value raises the current and can burn the start winding. Replace with the marked value and a voltage rating at least as high.

questions.q: With the new capacitor fitted, the pump starts but soon smells hot and trips its overload. What should Rushane look at next?
o: Whether the supply voltage is too steady for the motor
Whether the earth wire is too long for the motor to run
Whether the centrifugal switch is stuck closed in circuit
Whether the run winding reads higher than the start one
questions.why: If the centrifugal switch does not open, the start winding and capacitor stay in circuit, overheat and trip the overload. With the motor dead, read the switch contacts at rest and when moved by hand, as the maker advises. The overload is not to be set higher.

questions.q: What is the most likely reason the outdoor unit is silent, and what should Joel do about the contacts?
o: Salt and ants have damaged the contactor; replace it and seal the box
The capacitor's FAN section has failed, so the compressor must be replaced
The indoor fan is running, so the outdoor contacts must be healthy too
The compressor has a refrigerant leak, and the owner must deal with it
questions.why: White corrosion powder and an ants' nest in the contactor box are typical near the sea. Pitted contacts do not close properly and the outdoor unit never starts, while the indoor unit is on a separate supply. Replace the contactor like for like, remove the nest, and seal cable entries against insects and damp.

questions.q: The capacitor reads 45 µF on HERM and 5 µF on FAN. What does that show?
o: Both sections are in order, and HERM serves the compressor
The capacitor has failed, because the two sections differ so much
Both sections are in order, and HERM serves the outdoor fan
The capacitor has failed, because it should read 50 µF in total
questions.why: A dual run capacitor has two separate values, each with its own tolerance: 45 µF for the HERM (hermetic compressor) section and 5 µF for the FAN section, as marked. Both match, so the capacitor is good.

questions.q: Before touching the inverter board or capacitor, what must Joel allow for?
o: Nothing more, as the unit is isolated and proved dead
Stored charge in the capacitor, measured and then discharged
The unit's noise, which may startle him on the ladder at the time
The refrigerant pressure, which he lets out through the valve
questions.why: Capacitors and inverter boards hold a charge after switch-off. Wait the time on the label, measure the voltage across them and discharge with a resistor tool. The refrigerant circuit is never opened by an electrician.

questions.q: A pressure test later shows the compressor has seized and there is oil staining at a pipe joint. Where does Joel's work end?
o: He fits a larger capacitor so the seized compressor can turn
He recovers the refrigerant himself, once the unit is isolated
He hands the job to a certified refrigeration technician
He bypasses the compressor's overload to run it for a while
questions.why: A seized compressor and an oil stain mean a refrigerant circuit fault. Opening or recovering refrigerant is certified work, and bridging an overload on a seized compressor would burn the motor. The electrician reports the readings and hands over.

questions.q: What do the extractor motor's readings of 6.1, 6.0 and 3.4 Ω show?
o: All three windings are sound and well balanced
One winding has shorted turns and draws extra current
One winding is open circuit and has no path at all
The motor has been connected in star, not in delta
questions.why: The three windings should be nearly equal. Two at about 6 Ω and one at 3.4 Ω means the low winding has lost turns to a short between them. It draws more current, unbalances the motor and overheats it, so the overload trips.

questions.q: How should Tiana answer the customer's request for a bigger overload?
o: Fit it, since the overload is only a convenience device
Refuse: the overload is working; the motor needs rewinding or replacing
Fit it, and bridge the motor's thermal protector so it cannot trip again either
Fit it, but only if the customer signs for the extra risk
questions.why: A bigger overload would let the damaged winding overheat until the motor burns out, perhaps starting a fire. The overload is protecting the motor. Advise rewinding by a motor rewinder, or replacing with a motor of the same rating, frame and speed.

questions.q: Water is in the drum, yet the washing machine will not begin and its lock light stays off. Which part is most likely at fault?
o: The drain pump at the bottom of the machine
The bearings that support the drum
The door lock (interlock)
The water inlet hose at the back
questions.why: The cycle will not start until the door lock confirms the door is shut. A lock that never signals is the likely fault; it is a safety device, so it is replaced like for like, never bridged.

questions.q: The LED panel flickers, then switches off after a few minutes. The LED board itself is undamaged. What is the usual cause?
o: The metal ceiling grid holding the panel
The plastic diffuser cover on the front
The cover plate of the wall switch
The LED driver, which fails with heat
questions.why: The driver changes the mains supply to low-voltage DC for the LEDs, and it is the part that most often fails, especially in hot ceiling voids. Replace it with a driver that matches the board's current and voltage.

questions.q: What is the repair cost, with GCT at the current rate left out, as a fraction of the new freezer's price?
o: About 55%
About 34%
About 77%
About 183%
questions.why: 34,000 ÷ 62,000 = 0.548, about 55%. Both prices carry GCT at the same rate, so the fraction is unchanged. That is just over the common guide of half, so replacement deserves serious thought.

questions.q: What other facts should be put in front of the owner before a decision?
o: The age of the freezer's cabinet and the colour of any new one offered
Only the repair price, as the owner can see the new price in a shop
The colour of the technician's tools, and the day of the week
Remaining life, energy use, stock at risk and warranty
questions.why: An informed choice takes in more than the two prices: an old unit may fail again soon, a new one may use much less electricity, J$80,000 of stock is at risk, and a new freezer comes with a warranty.

questions.q: A 3 kW, 220 V instant water heater reads 9.5 Ω across its element with the supply off. What does this show?
o: The element is open circuit and needs replacing
The element is healthy: it should read about 16 Ω
The element carries 9.5 A whenever it is switched on
Part of it is shorted, or a parallel path is read
questions.why: R = V² ÷ P = 220 × 220 ÷ 3,000 = 16.1 Ω. A reading of 9.5 Ω is much lower: either part of the element is shorted, or the meter is reading through another parallel path such as a second element. Disconnect one end and retest.

questions.q: A 110 V ceiling fan runs slowly on every speed. Its bearings turn freely and its windings read as the maker says. The fan capacitor is marked 2.5 µF ± 5%. What reading shows it is still good?
o: Any reading above zero
About 1.4 µF
About 2.45 µF
About 4.0 µF
questions.why: 2.5 µF ± 5% is 2.375 to 2.625 µF, so only the reading of about 2.45 µF is within tolerance. 1.4 µF is a weak capacitor, and a larger value is also out of tolerance and changes the fan's current and speed.
